car.why: Car pace: characteristics blended into one score with weights from the track profile (aero tracks reward downforce, power tracks reward power and low drag). Each point above the reference score is 0.17% of lap time, so a 15-point gap between front and back of the grid gives the plan's 2–3%.

weightSPerKgPer90s.why: Seconds per kg per lap, scaled to a 90 s lap: 10 kg of excess weight or fuel costs ~0.3 s (plan 5.4).

driver.why: Driver pace: each point of pace above 88 is 0.045% of lap time, so the grid's 16-point spread is ~0.7% — smaller than the car spread, as in real F1. Form and morale around 70 nudge it; wet skill matters only on a wet track, up to 1.2% per 10 points at full wetness.

lapNoiseSd.why: Lap-to-lap scatter (seconds, sd), interpolated by the consistency attribute: grid drivers at 78–94 land in the plan's 0.2–0.4 s band.

fatigue.why: Fatigue 0..100 builds each lap, faster in heat and on high-g tracks, slower with stamina. Above 30 it costs 0.05 s/lap and +12% mistake chance per 10 points — a tired driver fades and errs late in a hot race (plan 5.16).

mistakes.why: Driver errors: ~0.4% per lap for a consistency-85 driver, far likelier in the wet and on the wrong tyre. Most are small moments; one in six is a spin, and one spin in seven ends in the barrier. Even the most consistent driver keeps a 0.05% chance per lap. How often a spin ends in the barrier scales with the track: ×(0.4 + 1.2 × SC profile), so walls close by (street circuits) turn errors into crashes and run-off forgives them.

start.why: Standing start: grid slots 0.2 s apart, 2.2 s lost accelerating from rest; the starts attribute gains or loses 0.02 s per point with 0.3 s of random spread; each car has a 1.2% chance of lap-1 contact.

traffic.why: A car cannot run closer than 0.3 s without passing. Within 1.5 s it loses up to 0.15 s per sector in dirty air, scaled by the track aero sensitivity and by the car: each point of dirty-air tolerance above 80 cuts the loss by 2%. Within 1 s the tow gives back up to 0.08 s per sector on straights. Lapping costs the backmarker 0.35 s and the leader 0.1 s. The aero-sensitivity scaling is (0.5 + sensitivity), so even a power track costs some time in the wake.

drs.why: DRS: ~0.3 s over a zone 12% of the lap long (scaled by the actual zone), for a car within 1 s at detection; enabled from lap 3 and off for two laps after a restart.

overtaking.why: Overtake probability is a logistic function: a sector's pace advantage in seconds, DRS, the racecraft gap, the tyre-wear gap and an ERS push raise it; a hard track to pass (overtakingDifficulty) and passing outside a DRS zone lower it. Failed attempts cost both cars time; about one attempt in eighty ends in contact. The pace advantage counts only up to 0.8 s per sector: a car that has run wide is not automatically passable on a narrow street circuit. A spun car is driven around, not overtaken. Away from a DRS zone a car only attempts when at least 0.25 s faster over the sector.

ers.why: ERS battery 0..1: recharges 0.35 per lap and an attack or a defence costs half a charge, so a car can push roughly every other lap. The system quality itself already counts in car pace (car.powerMix.ers); here it scales how much a push is worth relative to the reference deployment of 84.

fuel.why: Fuel use per lap is the track's figure, 0.4% lower per point of fuel efficiency above 83; cars fuel exactly to the flag plus a 1.5 kg margin.

pit.why: Pit stop = the track's pit-lane loss + a stationary time of ~2.5 s, 0.02 s better per point of crew quality above 80, with 0.2 s scatter and a 3% chance of a sticky wheel nut (+2–8 s). Under a safety car the whole stop costs 55% of normal, under a VSC 70%. No stop is quicker than 1.8 s stationary. A team without a chief mechanic counts as a 40-rated crew lead.

reliability.why: Mechanical failures per race = 0.45 × (1 − reliability): a 0.85-reliability car fails ~7% of races, close to real modern DNF rates. A third of failures are partial (0.9 s/lap slower to the flag); 60% come from the power unit.

damage.why: Contact: usually front-wing damage worth 0.8 s/lap until the next stop; a third of contacts puncture a tyre, one in five ends the race.

raceControl.why: Race control: a crash brings the safety car 10% + 90% × the track SC profile of the time, otherwise a VSC; a stranded car is usually handled with a VSC (12% + 30% × profile), sometimes the safety car; debris from contact sometimes a safety car. Background incidents (debris, stray objects) add ~0.5 × profile triggers per race. SC laps run 40% slower and the field closes to 0.8 s gaps; a VSC slows everyone equally. Calibrated so a track SC profile is roughly its share of races with a safety car, and the calendar averages ~40% (docs/calibration/M2.md). Behind the safety car or under VSC tyres wear at 40% and fuel burns at 60% of the racing rate. A car more than 1.5 bunch gaps behind the car ahead drives faster than safety-car pace to close up.

strategy.why: Strategist decisions: a plan 30 s slower than the best (a pit call 20 s worse) scores zero, so perception noise from decide.json means ~0.75 s of misjudgement for a top strategist and ~7 s for a poor one. Plans have up to 2 stops (3-stoppers are rarely right in the modern era; pit calls can still add a stop). A risk-loving strategist gets 0.02 per stop saved per unit of risk above 0.5, tipping near-equal plans towards fewer stops. Wetness moving by 0.08 triggers a tyre review; a safety car within 12 laps of a planned stop triggers a pit call. No planned stint is shorter than 5 laps. Below wetness 0.1 only slicks are considered; otherwise any compound within 6 s a lap of the best one for the conditions. Each stop also costs track position the car has to win back on the road: 15 s × the track overtaking difficulty — ~15 s where passing is nearly impossible, ~4 s where it is easy — so strategists stop less where they cannot pass.
